prize_parts.citation: For developing the political-economy theory of trade policy, showing how special-interest politics shapes protection and trade agreements.

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reading the other openings. The Grossman-Helpman framework turned lobbying and trade protection into a tractable, testable model and gave a disciplined account of why trade policy departs from efficiency. It has been used for three decades in theory, empirical work and trade-policy analysis. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: two names with a long, tightly coupled joint programme and a single canonical framework, so a two-laureate citation does not require arbitrary exclusions. Maturity is not a concern, since the core papers are from the 1990s. Their work on trade and endogenous growth strengthens the overall case, but I would anchor the citation on the political-economy contribution named in the ballot entry. I would also argue it on its scientific content, not on how many members ranked it first.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical. Support for the specific functional forms and structural parameters of the protection-for-sale model is mixed and sensitive to specification, so the contribution is arguably more a framework and research agenda than a settled set of findings. A second reservation is overlap with prior trade recognition (Krugman 2008) and with Helpman's role on the firm-heterogeneity ballot (B030), which could lead the committee to prefer the firm-level strand as the trade award. A third is that the growth-and-trade strand, which strengthens the pair's claim, sits outside this entry's stated discovery.

responses.point: Introducing firm heterogeneity and selection (Melitz 2003 and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extension) is a distinct advance beyond earlier new trade theory. It reorganised firm-level empirical work and has been tested heavily over two decades, which supports ranking B030 first.
responses.response: I agree B030 is a major, well-confirmed contribution and a serious alternative for a trade prize. My hesitation is attribution. Dreber Almenberg herself notes that the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum line, which established the exporter facts and parallel models, is not credited on the ballot, and Redding enters later. That leaves a visible gap that a clean award would have to resolve. The Grossman-Helpman credit has no comparable gap. Where we differ is on weighting: she weights the empirical reorganisation of the field, while I give more weight to a framework with unambiguous originators. I do not think the case is one-sided, and I would not call B030 weaker on scientific importance.

responses.point: The credit for B001 is concentrated in the Grossman-Helpman partnership, but empirical support for the protection-for-sale predictions is mixed and setting-dependent. The committee might prefer to reward trade through the firm-heterogeneity line instead.
responses.response: I accept the empirical caveat and list it among my own uncertainties. I would separate two questions. One is whether the specific equilibrium restrictions fit the data in every setting. The other is whether the framework changed how economists model and test the political determinants of trade policy. A framework that generates structural, falsifiable restrictions, even ones that are contested, is doing the work a prize-worthy contribution should do, and the mixed evidence is part of a productive literature. The risk would be a citation that overclaims. I would therefore word it narrowly around the political-economy theory, not around empirical validation of a particular specification.

responses.point: Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes demand estimation and dynamic industry models changed empirical industrial organisation. They are standard in merger review and antitrust, with about thirty years of validated use, and the attribution to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes is the clearest core.
responses.response: I did not rank B002 in my opening eight, so I should say plainly that I am responding to the argument, not to a view I held. The practical reach and maturity are impressive and I do not dispute them. Two things keep me from moving it above B001. Attribution has the hard limit he acknowledges: the credited list has seven names, and Bresnahan and Reiss, whom I would regard as foundational for empirical IO, fall outside a three-person award. And the contribution is primarily methodological, with continuing debate over identification assumptions. I do not treat methods prizes as lesser, but the weight of the case rests on the quality of the toolkit and its downstream use, and the committee should ask whether it identifies a single discovery. On that comparison I still find B001 somewhat cleaner.

responses.point: B018 combines new data and credible empirical designs with an explanatory framework on technology, tasks and trade shocks. It has had large policy influence and spawned much follow-on work. She places it first, with Autor, Hanson and Katz as the credited trio.
responses.response: I agree on policy relevance and on the empirical designs, which I ranked fifth. I differ on two points. First, attribution: her proposal includes Katz while many colleagues, including me, name Dorn. That divergence itself shows how uncertain the three-name cut is. The task-framework antecedents (Levy and Murnane, Acemoglu) are also not on the list. Second, maturity: the China-shock evidence is from 2013 onward, and the long-run size and persistence of the effects, along with the shift-share identification, are still being debated. I see that debate as healthy, but it argues for waiting for consolidation. It does not argue for ranking the work above a framework that has been absorbed for decades. This is a difference of weighting, and I could support B018 in a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would frame a trade prize around political economy and growth (B001) or firm heterogeneity (B030), and how Helpman's credit on both ballots should be handled.
Whether mixed empirical support for the protection-for-sale parameters is judged a limit on the discovery or a normal feature of a productive framework.
How far Krugman's 2008 prize and the 2025 growth prize overlap with the trade-and-growth strand, and whether the citation should include that strand.
Whether B003 or B050 would be a better first choice if the committee rates trade-policy theory as too narrow or too contested.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in matching, auctions and market design, and my listed collaborators do not include any credited name on B001, B003 or B050. My SSE affiliation alongside several committee colleagues is not a connection to any candidate.
